title: The Biggest First Day Of School Mistake You Can Make
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Through an extended narrative scenario, Linsin illustrates a subtle but consequential first-day error: letting minor lapses in a modeled procedure slide because students weren't technically 'misbehaving.' In his example, a teacher who had a great first day fails to enforce the end-of-day dismissal routine exactly as modeled, inadvertently teaching students that she doesn't always mean what she says. He argues this kind of small compromise snowballs, gradually eroding attentiveness, respect, and rule-following over the school year, and provokes teachers into escalating tactics like raised voices and lectures. The article then replays the same scenario with a correction: the teacher stops, waits silently for full attention, briefly restates expectations, and has students redo the procedure correctly before moving on. Linsin frames the first day as a uniquely powerful window, when students are most attentive and open, to establish that the teacher's word is reliable and that excellence is the standard for even mundane routines.
points: Never let a modeled procedure slide just because students weren't technically 'misbehaving'; small compromises signal you don't mean what you say.
When students don't meet an expectation, stop the class, wait silently for full attention, then have them redo it correctly before moving on.
Correct in the moment without lecturing or raising your voice; a brief 30-second review followed by a redo is enough.
Treat the first day as a uniquely powerful window, since students' attention and openness are at their peak and set the tone for the year.
Recognize the snowball effect: unaddressed small lapses grow into daily inattentiveness, disrespect, and rule-breaking over time.
quotes: But this one particular mistake will be responsible for scores of teachers getting off to a disastrous classroom management start—one many will never recover from.

Her students didn’t follow the end-of-day procedure like it was modeled, but because they weren’t technically “misbehaving,” she let it go. And this is where so many teachers who struggle with classroom management go wrong.

When you let things go, even seemingly innocent behaviors, it nudges a tiny speck of a snowball down a steep and bottomless hill. And the farther it gets down the hill, the more difficult it is to push it back up to the top.
As soon as the teacher notices that her students are not doing what was asked, she stops talking and stands in one place. She ignores the students approaching. She ignores the running.
After quickly reviewing her expectations (30 seconds), and without lecturing or raising her voice, she gives her signal for the class to do it again.
The mistake of course is ever going back on your word. If you say it, if you ask your students of it, then you must back it up with action.
